utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, just read it, that few lines, so that we are better able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I will do that willingly, but we are short of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Quite a lot of time on other issues. We would like to hear from you these 12 lines, and I will keep an eye on the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I will read the last part on page 17. [In English] "I think something strange happened to me during the time at the hospital. Sometime after I returned from Yugoslavia, I started having night dreams and flashes during the day. The image was always the same. I was standing beside -- beside the bed of one of the wounded soldiers and I looked over into the corner of the operating room. There was a sack, that is the only way to describe it, a stack of about five -- a stack of about five dead children, aged around 6 or 7." [Interpretation] The rest had been read out last time, Mr. President. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I am just wondering about hallucinations. You mean flashes during the day? That is what you refer to as hallucinations?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to return to your reaction immediately following this meeting that you allegedly had with Mr. -- with Captain Henneberry. Did you inform anyone of this?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. As I said on Friday, I accepted that that is what had been going on all the time. It was, in my words, not earth shattering at all. But I am not too sure, are you connecting this with the dream he supposedly had?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, Witness, I am not connecting anything with anything. I just want to know whether you -- whether you made some sort of official information. Your response to that is no, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I read your first statement very carefully which was given to the Office of the Prosecutor. Is it true if I say that, in that statement, you never mentioned that meeting with Captain Henneberry or the contents of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, is it true that you didn't mention, for the first time, the existence of this meeting with Captain Henneberry and the contents of that meeting, you didn't mention this until the 23rd of May, 2002, that is to say, until just a few hours ago?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Captain -- I apologise, Colonel. How is it that for a period of about 11 years, perhaps, you never remembered these facts and then all of a sudden, a few minutes before the first hearing, a few minutes before you were first questioned, you remembered this?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have tried to explain that when I arrived in Sarajevo and after watching the shelling that was going on, I concluded in my mind that there was a deliberate plan of shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I am going to interrupt you. I am going to interrupt you. I apologise. This conclusion that you have come to, wasn't it something that you could have thought of in 1997 or 1998 when you first -- when you gave your first statement?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, sir, but what Captain Henneberry was told me, it was not earth shattering. It was old news as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you answer the question as to why did you never mention this meeting and the contents of this meeting with Captain Henneberry before the 23rd of May, 2002?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it was not important. I had many, many important meetings. The information he told me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I am going to interrupt. I would like to continue, Mr. President, if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A lot of questions have been put to you regarding what you stated before and what you stated on the 23rd of May. Might it have been the case, or is it the case, that it came into your mind or came again in your mind on the basis of the information you received at that very moment from someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that could well have been the case because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then specifically ask you: Has the testimony of Mr. Henneberry come to your knowledge in whole or in part during what was said last week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say in part, Your Honour, if I may explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He reminded me of a time that he was very upset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who reminded you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Captain Henneberry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You spoke to him recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but he would not say what that was. I related this meeting, thinking that that is what it may have been. It is part of a jigsaw puzzle that I have often wondered about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you speak to Mr. Henneberry after he gave his testimony in this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told not to speak to him. We lived at the same hotel, sir, but we did not speak about any testimony. I made sure that he didn't and he had the same view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But as far as I understand, you have spoken about subjects which might have been part of his testimony. When you spoke about events that happened at that time in Sarajevo, you could never exclude that this would have been part of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what his testimony was, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it couldn't exclude that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. Our discussions were on things like how did the experience really affect us, as opposed to anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But your instructions were not to speak to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was told by my counsel not to discuss anything with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So by drawing the lines by yourself what would be relevant or not relevant, you more or less broke the instructions given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I am talking about -- we spoke before he gave his evidence. We were then told, when we was giving evidence, that there was to be no discussions, and there was not after that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have not been speaking to Mr. Henneberry after he gave his testimony, is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, spoke to him, sir, but nothing about Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just about the weather and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was living in the same hotel, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, these are the questions I was going to ask you but in a different manner, and I will go back to this subject. You just said a minute ago that you knew about Mr. Henneberry's testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that I did not know about his testimony, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That is what I heard you say, that you were partially acquainted with its contents?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will verify that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, tell you that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The response was to a very specific question which was as follows, a question by the President, [In English] "... come to your knowledge in whole or in part during what was said last week," and your answer was: "I would say in part, Your Honour." In part means "partially" in French. I shall reformulate my question once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you were aware of this testimony. You had partial knowledge of this testimony; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why did you say that you had partial knowledge of this testimony?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the fact that we were both here, as were others, giving testimony but I did not have anything from him --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, answer my question precisely. How is it that your memory was suddenly jolted about 11 years after the events and after you had stayed in the same hotel as the Witness Henneberry? And good day, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not told anything by Captain Henneberry in relation to this. All we discussed were how we generally felt after the event after 10 years. And I recall that he was very upset on a few occasions, and I often wondered why. I asked him why. He did not tell me because he said he was not allowed to speak about it. I shouldn't have perhaps asked him, but we didn't discuss anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But you spoke about a meeting at which he said that he was very upset; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I observed that he was very upset at one occasion when I visited Sarajevo -- Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am speaking about the recent events when you saw the witness Henneberry. And on how many occasions did you see him, Witness, in the last few days?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we crossed over as about three days, but we were not with each other, only at meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you are under oath right now. And can you state under oath in front of this Trial Chamber that you never spoke and never mentioned this famous meeting which you mention in the statement of the 23rd of May, 2002? Can you solemnly claim that this is the case?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You never spoke about it and you never even mentioned it, you never evoked it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have already said that I recall when I visited Lukavica that he was upset on one occasion. And he said, "Yes, I was," but he didn't go on and say why.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So would you agree with me in saying that you referred to it "partially"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would have to say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness. Witness, I would now like to return to these events. Who took the initiative to forward this statement of the 23rd of May, 2002?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement of the 23rd of May this year? The forwarded -- what statement is that one, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Took the initiative to establish this statement.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be my counsel, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You say "my counsel." Who is "my counsel"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You are saying that Mr. Mundis is your lawyer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be some misunderstanding, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. In a common law oriented system, a witness is more linked to one party, for example, because he is called by that party, than to another party. I don't think there is any use in continuing that line of questioning. We heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. That is right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So the initiative was taken by Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I had mentioned the incidents of which I think was recorded. For example, the statement by General Mladic at Christmas dinner. Are you referring to those statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, no. You know very well to what I am referring. Colonel, I am still speaking about the contact you had with Mr. Henneberry. You said in your statement of the 23rd of May, that this statement had been in a certain sense requested by Mr. Mundis. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, I think the witness may have become confused simply because of the fact that Mr. Piletta-Zanin refers to the supplemental information sheet as a statement. Again, this is not a document that the witness has signed or affirmed as being a statement but simply is information that we have provided for the benefit of the Defence based on information that the witness provided to us during a final phase of proofing. There is no evidence that the witness has signed this document, Mr. President, or has even seen this document, and I believe that's where partial -- the confusion may be partially coming from, in that my learned colleague keeps referring to this document as a statement when in fact the witness has not signed or read this statement, and it would be the Prosecution view that it is not a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In order to clarify this, Colonel Cutler, your interview, if it has been an interview, on the 23rd of May, the content of it, not in the form of a statement of yours, has been communicated to the Defence. So the Defence is aware of what has been the subject and probably the content of your discussions with the Prosecutor's office. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So we are speaking about this supplementary information about the 23rd of May of this year. Is it true that this information had been requested by Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made the statements and he recorded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell me when Mr. Mundis contacted you in order to do this?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been last Thursday or Wednesday afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So probably on Wednesday, sir, it was after you had already spent a few days in the company of Mr. Henneberry; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which meeting are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am still referring to the one of the 22nd of May -- sorry, the 23rd of May, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this building, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Have you been questioned about the subject -- when you were questioned about this subject, did the Prosecution use the term "plan"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Colonel, could you confirm if this is the case: That you only had very -- that you only had a very superficial knowledge of the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As a result, could you confirm that like in the case of Mr. Henneberry, you could only communicate through an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you said that you had met General Mladic on one occasion. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On two occasions, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Even better. Thank you. Sir, on each occasion, you had an interpreter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What was the name of the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jadranka Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Was she the interpreter of the Bosnian Serbs or of the military observers?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was hired by UNPROFOR to be interpreter for the military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Can you be certain of a translation, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jadranka Milanovic was very highly regarded as an interpreter and had very good scoring, as I understood it, in her testing. She was highly regarded by General Morillon, and I think she was basically in demand for any meetings that General Morillon had with General Mladic, General Gvero. I can only say, I think she was a loyal and faithful interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am interrupting you. You, yourself, in your capacity, how could you yourself personally judge about the quality of the work performed by Mrs. Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...because you don't understand their language. It doesn't need much explanation that you are not in a position to assess whether the interpretation is right or wrong. Of course, a line of two words cannot be translated into 100. There are a few exceptions. This really needs no explanation, unless you would like to know whether she was considered to be a good interpreter and that is what the witness answered. So please come up with --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I don't share your opinion, but that is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, have you ever, in the three months you spent in Sarajevo, knew of other occasions where you would be spoken to formally about a plan at the level of an army corps designed to produce what we have discussed earlier on; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I would like to go back to Sarajevo. Does the name "Zetra" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that what they called the Olympic stadium?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis. Please proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was the name of the Olympic stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know -- that is right. That is right. Do you know whether or a part of the Zetra hall had been transformed into a warehouse of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am personally not aware of that, but I would not be at all surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for your answer. In your statement of 1997 and 1998, you declared that the Bosnian forces possessed five tanks; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As said today --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Colonel. You also stated that each of these tanks could be used for firing; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I am sorry to be so quick, but we are short of time. Okay. So that they fired and that your answer was "yes." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You would have to explain the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Have you not stated, Witness, that the five tanks, although they were in bad condition, could nevertheless fire?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether they actually did that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you re-interpret, please? I missed the entire end of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether they actually fired, that the tanks actually fired?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Daily sit-reps would have recorded that. I cannot give you dates, times, and places, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, I would like to give you an exhibit which will be number 110. With the assistance of the usher, if Your Honour will allow me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We already have D110.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So it will be D111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wonder, but that is perhaps a question to Ms. Pilipovic before you change it. You introduced number D110 to refresh the memory of Mr. Cutler. It finally did not serve to refresh his memory. Would you still tender that, because there is nothing in the testimony of Mr. Cutler that finally could confirm, apart from that the letter exists, but whether the content is of any value. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would anticipate asking the witness a few questions in re-direct with respect to that document

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On D110. Okay, then perhaps D111 would be a better idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I just want to ask you for about 30 seconds for -- while we are dealing with these material considerations, I would like to ask you about a document which we will submit to you in a while, to please read point 5B. So you have a two-page document. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know about this document? Can you identify it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, does the name De Vere Hayes mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Does the form of this document remind you of anything?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The form of the document looks very much like what we would have used on our daily sit-reps, but I have not seen this one. I don't know where this one was from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That is all right. Let us presume, Witness, please, that the document, this document, which seems to be the number 00452672 -- 00452673 corresponds to one of these documents. Witness, please, could you read, please -- could you please read to us what you see on page 2 of the document next to the word "image," starting from the letter "B" which starts with the words "more probable."

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will read that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution objects. The witness says he has never seen this document and he does not know where this document came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to respond to Mr. Mundis, I see that the document was accepted a few days ago because it was recognised by a witness. The witness has now said that he cannot recognise this specific document but that it resembles one which has -- similar to the ones that he used for the sit-reps. And the number is ERN, so I think this is just a formal objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The mere fact that a document has an ERN number doesn't say that it could be introduced by any witness. So that is a different matter, whether finally the Prosecution would oppose against the use of the document. But, Mr. Mundis, would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I certainly would adopt what Your Honours have said but I would be curious as to which witness that Mr. Piletta-Zanin is referring to that has recognised this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not this document. He was talking about the admission of a document on the basis of recognition by a witness. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please refer to us exactly what, since that is the question of Mr. Mundis, what type of document you are -- was this a medical record or what type of document are you referring to? What witness were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I think that very recently in my absence, Ms. Pilipovic made an objection to a document that seemed unclear to her and I think that your Chamber said, that since the witness had in principle recognised it, there was no room for doubt and consequently you would admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A recognition in general terms, like "similar to." I think the witness also -- if at least you are very vague in what you say, but I don't remember anything else that the witness recognised the document also in relation to the content and not just in relation to the format. I don't think that the mere fact that a document has an appearance similar to documents known to a witness would be sufficient to ask any further questions. But apart from that -- but that might not be your mistake, that the document seems not to be complete, a few words missing. So, if you want to see whether any part of the content of the document or if you would like to ask any questions, you don't have to ask the witness to read if you say -- if the Defence would put that and then you can ask whatever question, but perhaps not in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you, Witness, read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we say not in relation to the document, you cannot ask him to read the document because that is the finest way of relating the question to the document. But you could perhaps read or paraphrase parts of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So I shall read, Witness, what is in front of you under "B," but before that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you not to relate the question to the document, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, so I said you could paraphrase but not in relation to the document because the witness doesn't know the document, and the only thing the witness has said is that it has a similar format.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember having had a meeting on February 15th, 1993, a meeting during which you referred to some strategic considerations and this custom with other military officers?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only meeting I think I had on the 15th of February was at Lukavica with -- besides the 8.30 conference that day, my UNMO meeting that evening, I visited Sarajevo -- Lukavica on that day to make sure that Colonel Marcetic had a letter that I had written in relation to the shelling of Papa 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: At that time or in the whereabouts of that time, is it not correct that those in charge of the UNPROFOR, that the strategy that the Serbs wanted was to guarantee an opening to the roads in Sarajevo and to ease tension and pressure in the city, with the aim of giving a map to Mr. Izetbegovic to avoid him using the media in the -- for the purposes he intended to? Would that -- does that remind you of anything? Does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis. Please proceed, Mr. Cutler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in relation to a meeting that -- I do not recall if it was the 15th of February but it was fairly close to that date. There was a meeting at the airport called by General Morillon, of which he wanted to declare a two-week ceasefire. That meeting was attended by General Mladic, General Gvero, the sector commander, General Morillon, of course, myself, and several other staff officers. That meeting was at the airport. It was supposed to have been attended by a Bosnian Presidency representative. I understand that General Siber was going to attend but a container had been put across the road going out to Sarajevo, and he refused to attend. The purpose of the -- the purpose of the -- the purpose of that meeting, I recall General Morillon trying to convince General Mladic that we needed a two-week ceasefire, during which time the utilities repair missions could get out and restore electricity to Sarajevo and to Pale and to Lukavica. It was during that meeting that I think General Mladic -- wrong -- General Morillon proposed a plan that President Izetbegovic wanted what was known as the "blue routes" out of Sarajevo. I was rather skeptical of that meeting, the reason being is there was not a Bosnian army representative there. And in any case, when we got Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. back that night, the shelling started again. General Morillon seemed to leave the meeting feeling as though we might have had a ceasefire. Unfortunately, that was not the case. If that is the meeting that you are referring to, then, yes, I recall that meeting quite well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for remembering that. Is it true, according to your knowledge, that the situation regarding the Serb position at the time was to try to ease pressure over Sarajevo, perhaps for political ends, but not to increase tension? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that was true at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir. Now I would like to speak about the situation of February 15, 1993. In respect of that meeting, you instructed your services to elaborate a chart of the opposing troops, of the opposing armies?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, I do not know what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Have you not, during that meeting of February 15th, 1993, gave instructions to your structures to work out a chart and a list of different commanders?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was part of what we were required to do. Whether I did it on the 15th or not, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I make an organisation chart? No. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall consult a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...of the instructions that you gave that such a chart was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. You are saying, did I give instructions that, as well as possible, UNMOs were to make up charts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Organisations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to clarify matters, I would like to give, and this is my very last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...quite clear to you. When you started your cross-examination, you had 50 minutes. You have taken now one hour and 20 minutes. Even if I deduct one and-a-half minutes for reading five lines and even if I would deduct all the questions I put in between and even if I would deduct such an important issue as what caused the witness to bring back into his memory certain events, even then, it took more than 50 minutes. So I will give you three more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, with the assistance of the usher, I would like to give you, if I have the permission, of page 11 of your statement that you will recognise. Could you tell me whether the signature is your signature?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On which page, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The page that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see is page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No. The number is at the bottom. Keep the page that you have in front of you there. Is that your signature, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not look like mine, but I am familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute between the parties about the document? If you perhaps, Mr. Usher, show it to Mr. Mundis, and please ask whatever question you would like to ask about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to read the part that has been highlighted in yellow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. "For this reason, my office compiled organisations and lists of commanders of the warring factions."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. We will have a break until 5 minutes past 6.00. I assume, Mr. Mundis, that the Prosecution needs to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an estimate on how much time you would take?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would say 5 to 10 minutes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five to ten minutes. Thank you very much. We will adjourn until five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin -- oh, you're -- then Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber that shortly before the break I indicated that I would be asking the witness some questions regarding Defence Exhibit 110. Upon reflection, the Prosecution has decided not to ask those questions. I am just informing you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, in response to some questions from counsel for the Defence, you described that you had had a partial awareness of Captain Henneberry's testimony. Can you describe -- just to be absolutely clear, can you describe once again the sequence of any discussion that you may have had with Captain Henneberry?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was something like this: I remember visiting Lukavica barracks one day on or after the 15th of February. I had already described in my main evidence that I regarded Captain Henneberry as a fine young officer. This particular day, he seemed very upset, and this is from my recall. I had never really been able to fathom out why he was so upset. And it was my recollection, by sitting down and thinking about the meetings that I had in Lukavica, that I had a recall of what he told me. As I said before, I asked Captain Henneberry not long after arriving here what his problem was, and he said he could not discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you there, Colonel. Do you recall approximately what day or date it was that you spoke here in The Hague with Captain Henneberry?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived here on the 15th. It would have been the evening of the 16th, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you continue with the discussion that you had with Captain Henneberry at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was basically it. I had been told we weren't to discuss anything. He said the same thing, he said we can't discuss it, and that is all there was to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Cutler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prosecution has no further questions for the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cutler, Judge Nieto-Navia has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Talking about the shelling of the Kosevo hospital --

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You said -- this afternoon, you said: "As I understand it, the only place that shell could have come from was from the Serbian side."

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: But reading your report of the 1st of February, 1993, and it is signed by you - it is Exhibit P745 - you said: "We are unable to determine exactly which battery was responsible for this shelling." Could you try to explain that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We are talking about two separate incidents. We are talking about the outgoing fire, the 9 rounds that were witnessed by the British colour sergeant, that was on the 11th of January. The incoming fire as a result of the rounds that were fired out, we could not establish where it came from, but in my mind, I knew where it came from, but I cannot prove that. Then there was the other incident of the 29th and 30th of January of which I had reports from Major Vassilev and Captain Baker. That is the one I was referring to, because there were 155 artillery mortar shells that landed in the hospital. The tail piece was kept as evidence, and to my knowledge, the Bosnian did not have 155 artillery pieces. That is why I made that statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi as one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. You mentioned incidents that took place when Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen visited, as well as when Mr. Boutros Boutros-Ghali visited Sarajevo. You said that, on this occasion, you had doubts as to whether the BH army positions -- you had doubts as to whether they had fired from the Presidency or by the Presidency. Is this just an assumption? Did you carry out an investigation? I would like to know how you came to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I did not state categorically where the fire come from. I was talking about the target was near the Presidency on those two occasions. It was strongly rumoured at the time that it may have been the Bosnians firing. I am aware that those two incidents were investigated, but I do not know what the conclusions or outcomes were, sir. It was strongly rumoured that the Bosnians fired themselves to draw attention to the fact that they were being shelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if I had understood you correctly, these were rumours, and they were rumours in the United Nations forces or were these rumours which its origin had not been determined?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were generally accepted, fairly strongly held rumours that that is what was going on within headquarter Sector Sarajevo and General Morillon's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would like you to tell me about the meeting which took place on the 15th of February, 1993. If I have understood this correctly, you said that this was in order to try and ease the siege of Sarajevo and that it was part of the BH army, it was the BH army side that was absent and that none was able or wanted to attend this meeting. And this idea of "easing" the siege, did this come from the Serbian side or did it come from the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting, sir, was called or initiated by General Morillon. He wanted the Serbian leadership, that is, General Mladic, and I think he wanted the senior supreme commander of the ABiH side to attend, so it was arranged that they would meet at the airport. The Serbian side was represented by General Mladic, General Gvero, and I think there were some other Serb officers there. Unfortunately, Colonel Siber who was going to represent the ABiH side was all prepared to come to the airport meeting, but there was a barrier had been placed across the road, I assume by the Serbian forces, and he refused to go any further. General Morillon started the meeting without the presence of Colonel Siber. He said to the Serb side, "either remove the barrier or come into the Sarajevo to the PTT and have the meeting," but General Mladic would not go into Sarajevo. As I understand it, the reason for the meeting was for General Morillon to convince both sides to have a two-week ceasefire in which time they could establish electricity into the city of Sarajevo and do other utilities repair missions. General Mladic did not think it was a right time to have a ceasefire but was prepared to assist in establishing what was known as "blue routes" out from the centre of Sarajevo through the area of Dobrinja to the airport and across, to allow women and children to go out of Sarajevo if they so desired. Because Colonel Siber did not turn up at the meeting, it was really one-sided. And the meeting broke up with General Morillon saying: "We have an agreement that there will be a ceasefire." I, as I said before, was not optimistic that that would be the case. That night, there was shelling on both sides. Have I answered the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, perfectly well. And just one clarification please, one last clarification. In your opinion, the "blue routes" which you mentioned which allowed women and children to leave the town, what did you think of the General Mladic's acceptance of this within the framework of the allegations made, let's say that he -- that in strategic he wanted to destroy the town or empty it of its Muslim inhabitants, and does that agree with these allegations?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The short answer, sir, is no, it doesn't. I was very skeptical of any such plan, although we all hoped and prayed that something like that would eventually occur. But it never came to anything. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sir, in your opinion, it was not serious or it had been put forward, it had been proposed, but not in order to be undertaken as an engagement, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion was that it was a very good idea, but it would not work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, I have one question for you as well. As I indicated before to you, an information sheet has been made of the last discussions you had with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and it refers to a meeting you had with Captain Henneberry when he was extremely upset. And the information sheet reads that he would have said that it was towards the end of your tenure.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can. I was very upset about the period of the shelling of Papa 5, and that occurred on the 13th and 14th of February. I went on CTO, that is leave, away from Sarajevo during the period 21 - 26 of February. Captain Henneberry took over the Lima headquarters post about the 29th of January. He would have only been in Sarajevo for a few days after I got back from CTO. So I can only conclude that the meeting would have been connected with the meeting I had with Colonel Marcetic, which I think was on the 15th. So it would be between the 15th and the 21st. I can't tie it down any tighter than that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you said between the 15th and the 21st. And you told us that afterwards -- well, do you remember what Mr. Henneberry then did? I just have to look in the transcript. One moment, please. Yes, I understand your answer. Thank you very much. That was the one question I still had for you. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would respectfully ask leave to ask a couple of follow-up questions with respect to questions put to the witness by Judge El Mahdi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is in relation to questions of the Bench, you know that usually this -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in total agreement because we are requesting the same thing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Prosecution is the first to ask any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi asked you a question. I am going to repeat the question and your answer, and the first part of your answer, and ask you if you are in a position to elaborate upon the answer you gave. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi asked you: "And just one clarification, please, one last clarification. In your opinion, the "blue routes" which you mentioned which allowed women and children to leave the town, what did you think of General Mladic's acceptance of this within the framework of the allegations made, let's say that he -- that in strategic he wanted to destroy the town or empty it of its Muslim inhabitants, and does that agree with these allegations?" Your answer: "The short answer, sir, is no, it doesn't." Are you in a position, Colonel, to elaborate upon your response: "No, it doesn't"? In other words, why doesn't that -- if you say: "No, it doesn't," why not?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I could not see the plan working at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which plan are you referring to, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The establishment of blue routes out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This discussion that you had with respect to the blue routes, this meeting about the blue routes, came after the Orthodox Christmas dinner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you able in your own mind in any way to reconcile the statements of General Mladic at the Christmas dinner with his position, vis-a-vis the blue routes?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent, I can, in that there seemed to be a shift on the Serb side away from not trying to do anything, to claiming that they would only fire into Sarajevo if fired upon first. And as I think I said on Friday, that certainly seemed to be the case at about that time. During that meeting at the airport which I discussed earlier, General Mladic's opening statement was in fact to that effect, that they would only fire if fired upon, and I well recall that. In fact, he made that point several times. And at that particular time, that certainly seemed to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Cutler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two very simple questions, sir. With regard to Papa 5, did you know whether near to this location at the time of these attacks, there were military positions, more or less mobile, of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution objects. This question does not seem to arise from questions posed by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is quite right, Mr. President. In reply to one of the questions that you asked, the witness said - I remember this clearly because I was very shocked - "during the attack on Papa 5." And he spoke about this. And on the basis of this reply, I am asking this question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, would you please reply to this question?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Marcetic had told me the reason they were firing on the area is that there was either a mortar position or a mortar OP in the area. I asked my UNMOs, was there, and they said not to their knowledge. But I certainly raised this matter with the ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. My second question: We spoke about the possible immigration of the weakest inhabitants of Sarajevo, women and children and the elderly, without a doubt. Do you know whether it is true that at the time in Sarajevo there were about 40.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "4.000"] Serbs in the interior of the city?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing surprises me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, I heard "quarante mille" instead of 4.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And to be even more precise, it seems that the numbers that we have been given, it is not 40.000 but a far greater number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were up to 100.000 Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would very, very much doubt that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I then take the opportunity to ask one clarification, so it is not a new question to the witness in respect of one of the answers he gave, I must admit not during these last questions, but earlier today on questions of Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Colonel Cutler, let me just read literally to you a part of the transcript and then ask for a clarification: At a certain question of Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you tried to get the question clearer and you said, about the sound of shells being fired: "Do you mean that there were fired out without being perceived?" Mr. Piletta-Zanin said, "exactly." Your answer was then "yes." You were asked about the possibility that the shells were fired without being perceived. So your answer was clearly "yes." The next question was: "Is it a probability or is it certitude?" It reads, "which is a certitude" but I think it was probability or a certitude. Your answer was: "Not a certainty, but it is certainly highly possible." The next question was: "So, consequently, it is perfectly probably -- or probable, that shooting from counter-batteries was triggered from Lima following firing from Sarajevo that had not been detected, yes or no?" Your answer was: "Yes." Then I read this part of the transcript. You first answered to the question given -- to the question is that you say, "It is highly possible, it is certainly highly possible that mortar shells could be fired without anyone hearing it."

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next question was: "Whether it would be perfectly probable or probably that shooting from counter-batteries was triggered from Lima following firing from Sarajevo?"

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not any more about the audibility, but it is about the probability that Lima was counterfiring mortar shells being fired from the city. So your answer, if I take it, your answer was "yes." That would mean that you say it is probable that the Lima firing was --

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in response to not-detected fire from the city. Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant to say, sir, was rounds being fired out of Sarajevo may not have been heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and they may have landed in, for example, Ilidza, and as a result, Serbs would respond into Sarajevo with fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would consider this very possible?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was possible, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But would you consider it probable that firing from the Lima side would -- well, let's say, usually be a response to undetected firing from the city, which is a different thing?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I understand the difference there, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first explain to you the difference. If there is a possibility that your response -- that there is undetected, unheard, firing from the city, that doesn't mean that most of the firing from the city would be unheard?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. No. Most of it would be detected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it therefore be correct, to understand your answer, that although there was a fair possibility that response fire to fire from the city would be a response to unheard-fire from the city, that you would not regard that as probable in most cases?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Most of the firing into the city was either on its own initiative or in response to "heard" shots going out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But possibly also against unheard shots?

utterances.speaker: JAMES PHILIPE CUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification to this answer. Mr. Cutler, this concludes your examination, your testimony in this court. Unfortunately, we could not finish your examination as a witness last Friday, but at least now it is Monday and we have finished. I thank you very much for having come to The Hague, having answered all questions from Prosecution, Defence, and the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Cutler out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P797, UNPROFOR report 14 February, 1993; Exhibit P797.1, English translation; Exhibit P809, under seal, UNPROFOR document; Exhibit P798, UNPROFOR report 13 February 1993; Exhibit P745, under seal, UNPROFOR report 01 February 1993; Exhibit D109A, agreement by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the concentration of all heavy weapons in and around Sarajevo; Exhibit D109B, agreement by the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the concentration of all heavy weapons in and around Sarajevo; Exhibit D110, letter from Dragan Marcetic dated February 2, 1993, in English; Exhibit D110.1, B/C/S translation; Exhibit D111, report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would object to Defence Exhibit 110 on the grounds that the witness was unable to refresh his recollection having looked at that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. If we were to disqualify all witnesses with a bad memory, there would be very many. This was a document addressed to Colonel Cutler. It is not a controversial document, and sometimes the witness's memory is excellent; sometimes it is at fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask for my information: The witness has testified that he received such a letter. I don't see that that is in dispute. What would be the additional probative value? I would just like to be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. One of the important questions is, and you have mentioned it, whether there was firing coming -- and here we have a very long list of heavy weapons and it would be useful to prove on the basis of documents of the time that one of the parties had certain weapons, to the extent that this can be contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, on page 21, line 14, this witness stated: "When I visited Mount Igman, I never saw one weapon except individual rifles." I believe, if I am not mistaken - and I very well might be - that that was in the context of this document being shown to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, but the very precise testimony of the witness was, if he hadn't seen weapons, knowing that they may have been mobile, there have been levelled spaces, grazed spaces, cut trees, that could be used as places for storing weapons. I think that this is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I prefer the Chamber to give a decision on the admissibility of this very document by the beginning of the court session of tomorrow. Is there any other document? No other objections? That means that the other documents under seal as far as mentioned by the registrar are admitted into evidence, and that on D110, a decision will be given by tomorrow. Mr. Mundis. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will take the next witness, Mr. Niaz, but before that happens, might I take this opportunity to indicate that there may be some difficulty later in the week with the proposed order of witnesses to be called by the Prosecution. In particular, Mr. Bergeron is due to be called after O'Keefe and before Thomas. I cannot confirm at this stage that Mr. Bergeron will in fact be here as anticipated. I will update the Trial Chamber and the Defence tomorrow morning. Mr. President, if he cannot attend later this week, I shall also make a proposal as to what witness or witnesses could be called instead so as to not lose time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can see, if cross-examination would just take as much time as examination-in-chief, that we still have 10 to 12 hours to go until Mr. Bergeron would appear. Is that correct or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We have reduced the anticipated time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do agree. I should not look in your letter of last Friday but in your letter of today. Yes. We will just wait first until tomorrow and see what will happen. If this would cause great difficulties to the Defence, we will hear from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness is Lieutenant-Colonel Afzaal Niaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, I seek to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Niaz, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration. The text will be handed out to you now by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Niaz. I have to inform you that your testimony will just take perhaps 10 minutes and then we have already to adjourn. But for reasons of efficiency, we try to use all the time. So for certainty, you will have to come back tomorrow. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, is your date of birth the 30th of March, 1957?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Have you been in the Pakistani army since 1977?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is your rank that of Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you serve in the former Yugoslavia as a United Nations military observer from the 2nd of October, 1993, until the 2nd of October, 1994?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Of that period, were you in Sarajevo as a United Nations military observer, or UNMO, from the 2nd of October, 1993 until March of 1994?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before leaving for the mission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry. Well, it is not for me to stand up to have the booth correct itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before leaving for the mission, did you receive some training in Pakistan?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Training as regard to what? Could you specify, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you receive any training in Pakistan before you left for the mission, that is, training for the mission itself?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Basically, it was a little orientation about the area and nothing specific. But I am trained as an infantry soldier for --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that. When you arrived in Zagreb, did you receive any training?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Yes. We had about four days or five days of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In what aspects?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Well, the -- first of all, we had to go to the driving procedures and orientation about the crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How much training did you have in crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Exact period, I would not be knowing but I think maybe about two to three hours. I am not sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. When you arrived in Sarajevo and commenced your duties as an UNMO, was that on the Lima side or the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: I was on the Papa side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you on various teams, various Papa teams, or one team?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: I was rotated on various Papa teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Which teams?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: My initial team was Papa 2. Then I served in Papa 4 -- not Papa 4, sorry. Papa 5, Papa 3, and also as an operation officer in Papa headquarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, indeed, at some stage did you become the team leader for the Papa 2 team?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Yes. I was, at the beginning of 1994, I was designated as Papa 2 team leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Which area did Papa 2 cover?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Papa 2, in fact, was located at Mala Hum. From there, if I correctly remember, Pofalici, some part of Sarajevo city, Dobrinja, area of Kosevo hospital. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you were a team leader, how many members did P-2 or Papa 2 have?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: The Papa 2 team varied from 8, and the maximum UNMOs I had in my team were 24. This was a special time when the weapons were being withdrawn from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What tasks did you have as an UNMO? In particular, I am interested in any tasks which had anything to do with sniping or shelling.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Well, our basic task was reporting, investigating any shelling or sniping activity inside the city or in, I would say, in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say "investigating any shelling or sniping activity," do you mean by that shelling or sniping of UN people or Bosnian army people or civilians, or some combination?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: As far as sniping of UN people were concerned, it was -- I remember it was only probably me who was sniped twice. About sniping of the Bosnian army was concerned, well, no. Yes, about the sniping of the civilian population, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What did you do by way of investigating the sniping of civilians?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Now, one of my duty was also to go to the hospital, Kosevo hospital and Dobrinja hospital, and the morgue in the Kosevo hospital at the end of the day, where I used to check the latest casualties in terms of injured and dead. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the state hospital in that regard? I think it is sometimes called the French hospital.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Yes. The hospital which was in the city, yes. But most of the time had gone to -- I was going to the Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And when you did that, did you carry out some sort of basic inspection of patients?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Yes. Because once I had to report that it was a sniping casualty or a mortar or shrapnel activity, I had to be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever carry out any investigations at the site of the alleged sniping of the civilians?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: No. Most of the time, once we were reported upon the sniping activity, the casualties were taken away, and once we used to go to the particular site, I have either pointed out by the local police of that area that this is the general direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So you relied on what the local police said in relation to the general direction of the source of fire; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: That is one. And the second is that we knew the general direction from where the fire was. Generally, the sniping activity was being carried out inside Sarajevo. So activity because small arm fire because sniping is very easy to pick up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again, in an effort to understand your answer, do you mean by that that there were notorious sources of sniping fire or do you mean something else?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: You are absolutely right because this activity used to be almost most of the time in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to incidents where civilians were allegedly shelled, did you carry out any investigations at the site of the alleged shelling?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were those investigations carried out by yourself or by team members, or by both yourself and team members?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: No. It had to be combination because a minimum UNMO which was supposed to go out were two. So at least it was two, me and somebody else from my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Over those months that you were in Sarajevo as an UNMO, how many shelling investigations did you carry out where the victims or victim were alleged to be civilians?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: It is very difficult to recall the exact number of these investigations. Maybe hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea in terms of an average per week or per day or per month, whatever is easiest for you?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: As average day would be, on the safe side, would be three, four.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to those investigations, on any occasion, did you establish a source of fire as being in an area controlled by the Bosnian government armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This seems a very general question covering a very long period of time, and it would seem difficult to discover a source in giving the large number of cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do press the question. In my respectful submission, there is nothing about that question which makes it inadmissible or lacking, in particular, lacking in probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, apart from it, may I understand the question that it is limited to the time where the witness was present in Sarajevo? That is more or less implicit, but since you gave no further time limit, the objection is denied. Perhaps you will repeat the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to those investigations, that is, those carried out by you and team members, or you or team members, on any occasion, was a source of fire established as being in an area controlled by the Bosnian government armed forces?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace. As I told you, Mr. Niaz, it would be only short for today, but we will adjourn until a quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
